title: Steinberg endomorphisms detect a nonzero fixed vector
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $S$ be a semisimple simply connected $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Semisimple means smooth, affine, connected and of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, where solvable means that the successive commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. Simply connected means that every surjective homomorphism $S'\to S$ from a semisimple group scheme with finite central kernel is an isomorphism; finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and central means commuting with every element after every scalar extension. A finite-dimensional rational $S$-module is a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $U$ with linear coaction $\rho_U:U\to U\otimes_F F[S]$ satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity. Write $U^S=\{u:\rho_U(u)=u\otimes1\}$. For every such $U$ and every $0\ne x\in U^S$, there exist a nonzero finite-dimensional rational $S$-module $E$ and an equivariant $F$-linear map
$$\varphi:U\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_F(E)$$
such that
$$\varphi(x)\ne0,\qquad \operatorname{End}_F(E)^S=F\cdot\operatorname{id}_E.$$
Here $\operatorname{End}_F(E)$ is the vector space of linear endomorphisms with conjugation action: for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$, $s\in S(A)$ acts on $a\in\operatorname{End}_A(E\otimes_F A)$ by $a\mapsto s a s^{-1}$. Equivariance and invariance are identities of coactions, not just identities for $F$-points. The statement includes characteristic zero and every positive characteristic, as well as $S=1$.

They are finite-dimensional rational $S$-modules. This supplies the split data needed in the representation-theoretic lemmas over the given algebraically closed field, without assuming a split form as an extra hypothesis.

source.place: Lemma 9.7.4(1),(2) combined with the all-sufficiently-large quantifier in Lemma 9.7.2(2).

proof.text: Define $\Theta:E\otimes_F E\to\operatorname{End}_F(E)$ by $\Theta(u\otimes v)(w)=d(v)(w)u$. For a basis $e_i$ with dual basis $e_i^*$ its inverse sends $A$ to $\sum_i A(e_i)\otimes d^{-1}(e_i^*)$: composing on $w$ gives $\sum_i e_i^*(w)A(e_i)=A(w)$, and composing on $u\otimes v$ gives $\sum_i d(v)(e_i)u\otimes d^{-1}(e_i^*)=u\otimes v$. For every $F$-algebra $C$ and $s\in S(C)$, equivariance of $d$ gives $d(sv)(w)=d(v)(s^{-1}w)$, so $\Theta(su\otimes sv)(w)=s\Theta(u\otimes v)(s^{-1}w)$. Therefore $\Theta$ is equivariant for the diagonal action and conjugation action. Put $\varphi=\Theta\circ a$. It is equivariant and $\varphi(x)\ne0$ because $a(x)\ne0$ and $\Theta$ is injective. All displayed identities also hold at the universal point of $S$, hence are coaction identities.

source.place: Theorem 9.7.5, tensor-to-endomorphism identification; agent-written basis inverse and universal-point equivariance.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-rho-tensor-square-invariant-line], $(E\otimes_F E)^S$ has dimension one. The equivariant isomorphism $\Theta$ and its equivariant inverse restrict to inverse linear maps on invariant subspaces, so $\operatorname{End}_F(E)^S$ also has dimension one. The identity is invariant since $s\operatorname{id}_E s^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_E$ after every scalar extension, and is nonzero since $E\ne0$. A one-dimensional vector space is spanned by any nonzero vector, hence $\operatorname{End}_F(E)^S=F\operatorname{id}_E$. Together with Step 4 this proves every clause.
